articles.text: Editor: In my opinion, the state legislature should not have viewed the solution to our housing shortage based on individual cities. A regional approach to this problem is far more rational. It is my understanding that no consideration was given to the available space that each city has to accommodate new high density housing. In the case of Piedmont, the only available open sites are our very limited parks and recreational fields. I think we should pursue having the state legislature have a carve out for cities, such as Piedmont, instead of having to sacrifice or precious, open green space of which we have so little. Our city officials and the citizens at Piedmont need to contact our state legislators. It’s obvious that in recent years we have seen a tremendous number of residential housing units built in Oakland and Berkeley, San Leandro and Hayward, El Cerrito and Richmond, which have the open space needed to accommodate this high density housing. Some people prefer living in a high density housing situation. I am not one of them, and I don’t think most people in Piedmont are either. Putting 160 units in Blair Park is an absolute abomination. This project will change the whole feel of the Morgen Canyon. Na is an obscenity. This is a natural green corridor and should be preserved forever and not degraded in order to comply with a poorly thought out housing mandate from the State of California. This particular site gets very little natural sunlight. Moraga Avenue of course is a major thoroughfare for emergency access and egress from the hills should there be another fire, and this will be significantly compromised . The Coaches Field location is at least a little bit more removed and we’ll have less of an impact on the canyon because of this. It is also a more expensive project which would make it less likely to be built Again, I think we need our city officials to pursue the idea that to carve out for cities that have no open space, parks and green belts should be off limits. Loss of the little green space we still have in Piedmont will detract from our health and well-being immeasurably. –Alan Cohen Maxwelton Rd., Piedmont

articles.text: I recently lost a ring. It was a simple gold band with small ridged edges. It was my mother’s original wedding band, She had given it to me at the beginning of my sophomore year of high school. In other words, that simple golden ring had been with me on my pinky finger for the majority of my life in high school. Any time I felt myself becoming anxious before an exam, nervous before a tennis match, or even when I was just fidgety, I would start to twirl the ring that sat on my pinky finger. The ridged edges would contrast the smoothness of the band itself, and I would become grounded in the feeling of twisting it around my finger. Facing ever-changing friend groups, failed assignments, choir rehearsals, late night froyo runs with my best friend, and even the death of my grandmother, my mother’s ring was on my finger. In essence, while the world around me failed to stay consistent, the ring on my finger never changed. Its weight was a reassurance for whatever I faced next. It had traveled with me around the world and back. From Edinburgh, Scotland to Cancun, Mexico to Tahoe City, California. Through customs, airports, airplanes, hotels, bus rides, cab rides, museum explorations, dinners by the beach, roller coasters, and so many other experiences, the ring stayed firmly on my finger. I leave for college in five days. The thought that the ring wouldn’t come with me hadn’t even entered my mind — why would it? The ring had gone everywhere with me, what was one more adventure? In my panic to find the ring, I realized my panic wasn’t solely about misplaced jewelry, but instead a projection of my fear of leaving for college. It was the fear of change; change on such a monumental level. The next four years of my life would be spent nearly 5,120 miles away from home. The ring would be a reminder of home, of my family. This fear kept me tossing and turning in the stale air of my bedroom most of the night. As much as I want to go to college and experience what many label as “the best four years of their life,” I have to admit that I am scared. I have spent 18 years in the same house, in the same room, surrounded by the same people talking about the same things. The fear of starting over is strong and can be paralyzing. But the fear of not trying my best to make the most of my brand new start is stronger still. Ring or no ring, I am going to college. And while I consider myself to be deeply superstitious (irrational), and just slightly religious (rational), I briefly took the ring’s disappearance as a bad omen. That line of thinking came from the superstitious part of me, but the religious side tells me the loss of a material item doesn’t translate to something bad happening. I now find myself faced with a dilemma. I can either remake the ring with unused gold jewelry from my mother, or I can just move on. The rational part of my brain tells me that there are so many material things that remind me of home that I can’t take with me to college. For example, the flickering street lamp on Hagar Ave where my best friend and I watched the sunset, or the cutting boards that had Slavic imagery on the backs that my mother would use when she cooked, or even the painting hanging on my wall of an antique Italian car race advertisement that my father got for me. There are so many things that I can’t take with me; I can only take their memory and their significance, knowing they are waiting for me to come back home. But I have the opportunity to take the ring with me, even though I know it won’t be the one I had. So the new question is, do I remake the ring and take the familiar weight on my pinky with me to college, or do I go to college and start anew without its company? I think only Plato has an answer. But unfortunately for me, he is long dead and I don’t speak Greek. To channel some of my own philosophy, I say that this decision is inconsequential. Compared to what I will one day inevitably be faced with, this is child’s play. In six months my life will be so drastically different this decision won’t matter. So I say, a ring is just a ring. Whatever memories I had with it aren’t exclusively tied to that piece of gold. They exist in my mind. And if I remake the ring, it’s because I miss the jewelry itself and not the made-up significance in my mind. While I didn’t end up remaking the ring, I admit I did buy a replacement. I will never forget my mother’s wedding band and its comforting presence throughout the highs and lows of high school. But the new ring serves as a clean slate, ready to experience new adventures – and new memories. Larissa Edel has been a contributing writer with the Post for six years and soon will begin college at University of St. Andrew’s in Fife, Scotland.

articles.text: The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) has published a Draft Environmental Impact Report (EIR) for an upcoming Pacific Gas & Electric (PG&E) power-line replacement project. To provide information about the proposed project, CEQA process, and provide an opportunity to submit verbal comments, the CPUC will hold two virtual meetings on Wednesday, September 3, at 2:00 p.m. and at 5:00 p.m. The Draft EIR evaluates potentially significant adverse environmental impacts that could be associated with the Project and identifies project components, mitigation measures, and project alternatives that would avoid, reduce, or eliminate significant impacts. The EIR ends its 45-day comment period on Friday, September 26. Officially called the “PG&E Moraga-Oakland X 115 Kilovolt (kV) Rebuild Project,” the proposed project is a maintenance project intended to replace older existing 115 kV power line equipment that has reached the end of its useful life. Upon completion of construction, the structures currently in place would be replaced with more fire-resistant structures and conductors. Citizens may attend the virtual meetings on September 3 with the following Zoom links: • 2 p.m. - https://us02web.zoom. us/j/84794642276 • 5 p.m. - https://us02web.zoom. us/j/89981865478 Project Background The proposed project involves upgrades to approximately five miles of overhead 115 kV power lines between Moraga and Oakland X substations in the City of Orinda, unincorporated areas of Contra Costa County, and the cities of Oakland and Piedmont A map shows the length of power line to be replaced in the proposed plan. within Alameda County. The project seeks to rebuild the four overhead lines into four hybrid lines, with both overhead (about 4 miles) and underground (about 1 mile) segments. Existing towers, poles and conductors would be replaced either with overhead rebuild or underground components, and minor modifications would occur within the existing substations. Some recently replaced power line structures would be reused or reused with some modification. The CPUC is the lead agency responsible for environmental review of the project in compliance with the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). According to the CPUC, the operation of new overhead and underground power lines in this project would reduce the risk of wildfire compared to existing conditions. Written comments may be submitted for inclusion in the final EIR via email at MOX@ aspeneg.com before September 26. Comments should reference the Moraga-Oakland X Project, A.24-11-005. Before including an address, phone number, email address, or other personal identifying information in their comment, residents should be aware that their entire comment will be placed in the Project file and shall become part of the public record. Comments are also posted online as part of the public record. The CPUC cannot approve requests to withhold contact information from the public record. It was a simple gold band with small ridged edges. It was my mother’s original wedding band, She had given it to me at the beginning of my sophomore year of high school. In other words, that simple golden ring had been with me on my pinky finger for the majority of my life in high school. Any time I felt myself becoming anxious before an exam, nervous before a tennis match, or even when I was just fidgety, I would start to twirl the ring that sat on my pinky finger. The ridged edges would contrast the smoothness of the band itself, and I would become grounded in the feeling of twisting it around my finger. Facing ever-changing friend groups, failed assignments, choir rehearsals, late night froyo runs with my best friend, and even the death of my grandmother, my mother’s ring was on my finger. In essence, while the world around me failed to stay consistent, the ring on my finger never changed. Its weight was a reassurance for whatever I faced next. It had traveled with me around the world and back. From Edinburgh, Scotland to Cancun, Mexico to Tahoe City, California. Through customs, airports, airplanes, hotels, bus rides, cab rides, museum explorations, dinners by the beach, roller coasters, and so many other experiences, the ring stayed firmly on my finger. I leave for college in five days. The thought that the ring wouldn’t come with me hadn’t even entered my mind — why would it? The ring had gone everywhere with me, what was one more adventure? In my panic to find the ring, I realized my panic wasn’t solely about misplaced jewelry, but instead a projection of my fear of leaving for college. It was the fear of change; change on such a monumental level. The next four years of my life would be spent nearly 5,120 miles away from home. The ring would be a reminder of home, of my family. This fear kept me tossing and turning in the stale air of my bedroom most of the night. As much as I want to go to college and experience what many label as “the best four years of their life,” I have to admit that I am scared. I have spent 18 years in the same house, in the same room, surrounded by the same people talking about the same things. The fear of starting over is strong and can be paralyzing. But the fear of not trying my best to make the most of my brand new start is stronger still. Ring or no ring, I am going to college. And while I consider myself to be deeply superstitious (irrational), and just slightly religious (rational), I briefly took the ring’s disappearance as a bad omen. That line of thinking came from the superstitious part of me, but the religious side tells me the loss of a material item doesn’t translate to something bad happening. I now find myself faced with a dilemma. I can either remake the ring with unused gold jewelry from my mother, or I can just move on. The rational part of my brain tells me that there are so many material things that remind me of home that I can’t take with me to college. For example, the flickering street lamp on Hagar Ave where my best friend and I watched the sunset, or the cutting boards that had Slavic imagery on the backs that my mother would use when she cooked, or even the painting hanging on my wall of an antique Italian car race advertisement that my father got for me. There are so many things that I can’t take with me; I can only take their memory and their significance, knowing they are waiting for me to come back home. But I have the opportunity to take the ring with me, even though I know it won’t be the one I had. So the new question is, do I remake the ring and take the familiar weight on my pinky with me to college, or do I go to college and start anew without its company? I think only Plato has an answer. But unfortunately for me, he is long dead and I don’t speak Greek. To channel some of my own philosophy, I say that this decision is inconsequential. Compared to what I will one day inevitably be faced with, this is child’s play. In six months my life will be so drastically different this decision won’t matter. So I say, a ring is just a ring. Whatever memories I had with it aren’t exclusively tied to that piece of gold. They exist in my mind. And if I remake the ring, it’s because I miss the jewelry itself and not the made-up significance in my mind. While I didn’t end up remaking the ring, I admit I did buy a replacement. I will never forget my mother’s wedding band and its comforting presence throughout the highs and lows of high school. But the new ring serves as a clean slate, ready to experience new adventures – and new memories. Larissa Edel has been a contributing writer with the Post for six years and soon will begin college at University of St. Andrew’s in Fife, Scotland. If I climb the highest mountain you are there and yet if I find myself in the lowest valley of my life, you are there. Teach me today to love you more and help me to rest in the “enoughness” of your grace. Amen. articles.text: On Monday, September 1 Children’s Fairyland turns 75 and will celebrate with a full day of family fun from 10 a.m.- 4 p.m. The Labor Day event will feature performances by DJ Lance Rock, Prescott Circus, Daisy the Clown, with hands-on activities, interactive art, a brand-new bilingual puppet show, giveaways, special guests, and a parade through Oakland. “This isn’t just a birthday party, it’s our love letter to the generations of families that have supported Children’s Fairyland,” said Kymberly Miller, CEO of Fairyland. “For 75 years, Fairyland has been a place where kids and families fall in love with storytelling, make cherished memories, and feel safe to play, explore, and connect. This celebration honors our past, reflects on our growth, and opens a new chapter in Fairyland’s story.” The 75th Birthday Party kicks off at 9:30 a.m. with a Parade to the Birthday Party, co-hosted by BART and Fairyland. Starting at the 19th Street BART Station, the parade winds its way to Lake Merritt and ends at the Fairy Gates. DJ L a nce Ro ck , t he Emmy-nominated host of the hit Nick Jr. Series “Yo Gabba Gabba!,” brings his signature mix of music, storytelling, and dance to Fairyland’s Festival Stage. He’ll perform live twice, at 1:00 p.m. and 3:00 p.m., each followed by a meet and greet. Learn more about DJ Lance Rock at www. djlancerock.org. The birthday party will also premiere “Tío Conejo’s Big Wish,” Fairyland’s first fully bilingual puppet show based on a folktale from Cuba. The show will run through October 26, with daily performances at 11:00 a.m., 2:00 p.m., and 4:00 p.m. A live show by Prescott Circus at noon featuring Oakland youth performers showcasing acrobatics and juggling. A bubble-filled performance by Daisy the Clown at 2:30 p.m., blending balloon twisting, magic, and playful chaos. Daisy is a beloved performer known for creating interactive and creative fun for kids of all ages. Puppet Playdates with Quercus, Fairyland’s fuzzy mascot, occur at 11:20 a.m. and 2:20 p.m. Children’s Theatre interactive performances of “Teddy Bear’s Wish” start at 11:30 a.m. and 12:30 p.m. Plenty of activities, including interactive art stations, a giant birthday card for Fairyland, a community-painted mural, a Birthday Adventure Passport activity, where kids collect stamps after completing activities and prompts, then turn it in for a limited-edition 75th anniversary button. All kids will take home special goodie bags. On September 2, 1950, Children’s Fairyland opened its gates as the country’s first storybook theme park, built specifically for young children. Fairyland quickly became a cherished part of Oakland’s identity and cultural landscape, igniting imaginations, shaping childhoods, and inspiring countless theme parks around the world. The idea for creating a storybook theme park in Oakland began in 1948, when local nursery owner Arthur Navlet envisioned a place where children could play freely and safely through a world built just for them. With support from the Lake Merritt Breakfast Club, Oakland Parks Superintendent William Penn Mott Jr., and a dedicated group of community members, the dream for Children’s Fairyland took shape. Since then, Fairyland has remained a cherished part of Oakland’s cultural landscape, attracting nearly 200,000 visitors annually to explore the park’s 10 acres. Over the years, it has grown to include cultural celebrations, literacy programs, puppet education, summer camps, and one-of-a-kind performances that reflect the diverse cultural heritage of the Bay Area. The park has remained true to its roots over the decades, providing hands-on, screen-free experiences that inspire imagination, creativity, confidence, and a lifelong love of learning. Buy tickets in advance at Fairyland.org Celebrate 75 years of Fairyland on Labor Day, September 1.

While Piedmont remains the largest participant, the most dramatic growth occurred in neighboring communities, with Oakland registrations jumping 16% and Berkeley increasing its participation by 44%. The FIRST LEGO League Challenge division for older students (4th-8th grade) led the surge with nearly 40% growth from 257 to 350+ participants, demonstrating both strong community appeal and the magnetic pull of hands-on STEM education that extends far beyond Piedmont’s borders. This year will mark a change in leadership, as long-time co-founder Dave Ragones stepping down from the presidency. While continuing to participate as Treasurer, Ragones leaves an indelible mark as co-founder and leader of the Piedmont Makers. Ragones’s efforts are well known within the community, as highlighted by PUSD’s recognition in 2023, honoring Ragones with the Arthur Hecht Volunteer of the Year award. articles.text: From therapy sessions to healthy snacks, the PUSD Wellness Center plays a vital role in student well-being. This year’s fundraiser will help ensure these services remain free and accessible for Piedmont middle and high school students. The Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) Wellness Center has officially launched its 2025 fundraising campaign, aiming to raise $50,000 to continue providing essential mental health services to Piedmont’s middle and high school students. This year’s campaign is off to a strong start thanks to lead donors Tom Snyder and Anne Bisagno, who opened the campaign with a $10,000 contribution. Their early support sets the tone for a community-wide effort to ensure the PUSD Wellness Center can maintain its current level of care. The Wellness Center (WC) is a vital resource for Piedmont High School, Millennium High School, and Piedmont Middle School students, offering therapeutic support for challenges such as stress, anxiety, depression, grief, conflicts, and substance use concerns. During the 2024–2025 school year, one in three students at Piedmont and Millennium High Schools and one in four at Piedmont Middle School visited the Wellness Center. Last school year, WC therapists provided more than 2,000 therapy sessions, while over 150 students received ongoing, individualized support. The Center also offered more than Staff photo Wellness Center therapists Emily Goodwin (left), Kimmy Demkovich and Umara Hansen, Wellness Center co-founder Brooke Zimmerman and Wellness Center therapist Jen Blau 3,500 healthy snacks to students, provided practitioner training led by top mental health experts, and remained a trusted place for both scheduled and drop-in care. “The availability of a free, on-campus Wellness Center is an essential resource for our students,” said School Board President Lindsay Thomasson. “It removes significant barriers to accessing mental health care, including the difficulty of finding an available provider, scheduling appointments, and managing outof-pocket expenses.” The Wellness Center operates on a minimal budget, with community donations funding critical staff stipends, program supplies, and student support activities. Every contribution, large or small, helps support this safe space for Piedmont students to seek support and build resilience. Major corporate donors to the 2025 PUSD Wellness Center fundraising campaign thus far include Elfster and Hillside View Orthodontics. Aspen Grove Adolescent & Young Adult Medicine, Piedmont Pediatric Dentistry and Revive Health Therapy have also given in support of the Center. Individual donors who give $500 or more by October 1 will receive an invitation for two to the Wellness Center Sponsor Reception at a private home in Piedmont on October 9, featuring a moderated panel of teen mental health experts. Major donors at levels above $1,000 will have their name added to the gratitude wall in the Wellness Center at Piedmont High School. To contribute to the 2025 campaign or learn more about the Wellness Center’s programs, please visit Piedmontwellness.org.

articles.text: Piedmont football returns this Saturday with a season-opening game at Salesian. Piedmont football is back this Saturday, August 30 with an opening game at Salesian in Richmond to kick off its 10-game season. The Highlanders return after going 10-2 in 2024 with a senior-laden squad that won its first North Coast Section game since 2017. It sought its second straight Western Alameda County Conference Mission Division title and won its third league banner in as many years. “We’re still in the middle division with Hayward and Newark Memorial. It’s going to be a physical year just like it was last season. Hayward brings a similar team but is new in some spots. They are already talking a lot,” said Piedmont coach Jordan Seiden. Piedmont lost 16 players to graduation in the Class of 2025, requiring obvious overhauls to both offensive and defensive units. “15 of those 16 players were two-way starters. Now it’s a whole new cycle. We’re doing a lot of teaching like we did the first couple of years. It’s a young group, but they are going to be good,” Seiden said. For a fourth year, Piedmont will have a Lagios at quarterback wearing No. 4. This time, sophomore Jimmy Lagios steps into the starting role following the graduation of his older brother, Markos. Incoming quarterback Jimmy Lagios talks things over with coach Jordan Seiden. Rehan Mumtaz carries the ball in running back drills at practice. Staff Photos “Jimmy had a great year on JV, we want to see his growth and development. As that’s happening, he’s going to be a huge part of anything we’re able to do. It’ll look differently offensively. He’s not as mobile as Markos was, but he’s a natural smooth thrower. Same number, they look alike, but he’s taller. They are different and similar at the same time,” Seiden said. On offense, PHS must replace starting running back Tommy Ashton and star receiver Sam Shelby, an honorable mention for the Post’s Athlete of the Year award. At running back, Piedmont could have a formidable threeheaded monster with Xavier Henderson, Colby Hong, and Rehan Mumtaz. Hong and Henry Brennan will also fill into the inside linebacker spot vacated by Ashton, while Henderson will continue at linebacker as well. Jack Meyjes and Dash WatersWorthen will take the lead at receiver, Meyjes will also play defensive back. “Xavier is one of our more vocal leaders. We also need Colby and Henry to be the quarterbacks of our defense and be vocal. That leadership will manifest itself. We’re young, so people will have to step up as leaders,” Seiden said. Despite losing the vast majority of starters from last year, Piedmont will still have leadership with eight seniors from the previous team. Adrian Kondakov and Bill Ashton make two critical pieces to their offensive and defensive lines. “We have a great coach in Oski Tauaho, and Adrian has fed off of Oski’s energy and the teaching he’s gotten from him. Adrian is one of my four-year kids and he doesn’t say much, but he leads by example,” Seiden said. After visiting Salesian this Saturday, Piedmont will travel to Middletown on September 5 and have their home opener at Witter against Berean Christian on September 12. articles.text: Ryan Tripp (left) details his rowing career after his boat with Dartmouth won the silver medal at the IRA National Championships. Ryan Tripp graduated from Piedmont High in 2020 and closed his collegiate career at Dartmouth in monumental fashion. He helped his college lightweight eight win the silver medal at the Intercollegiate Rowing Association National Championships on June 1. Dartmouth finished less than a boat length behind Harvard in a field of six schools. Following nationals, Tripp was among three nominees for the inaugural Oarsman of the Year Award, considered the Heisman Trophy of rowing. Helped by Tripp, Dartmouth’s silver medal is a testament to their perseverance as a program. It was the school’s first medal in the event in 12 years. Back in 2020 Dartmouth dropped the lightweight rowing team amidst budget deficits caused by COVID-19. It was reinstated in 2021. “When we came into the fall of 2021, we took on a lot of novices and people who were trying out rowing for the first time. My freshman year was a season with a lot of ups and downs. We saw some glimmers, like placing fifth at the Head of the Charles,” Tripp explained. “We were steadily making progress on paper, but I don’t think we won a race as a freshman or as a sophomore. We had to keep a level head and slowly build a culture that loved training and supporting one another. We knew we’d have to weather losses and hard times,” he added. Tripp was the only senior in Dartmouth’s silver medal winning boat. After the National Championship race, head coach Trevor Michelson spoke of Tripp’s leadership helping propel their boat to the podium. Tripp said he tried to replicate things he learned from captains before him. “One of the great gifts is being able to learn from everyone you train with. There’s something really unique with how we cared for one another. It was so clear that we had a shared commitment, so I wanted to keep harping that and making sure everyone felt extremely supported,” Tripp said. In the weeks that followed, Tripp wrote a detailed reflection of his 10-year rowing career, offering unique insights that could prove valuable to other young athletes. He wrote about the importance of genuinely caring about the wellbeing of teammates, a shared unwavering fixation on setting records at Dartmouth, grounding yourself by reflecting on your past, and the various mentalities related to sport. “We used that metaphor to keep medaling at national championships on our horizon for a very long time. We were focused with the training. The team was motivated and you have to be comfortable rowing in those competitive scenarios,” Tripp said. Tripp wrote about times in his rowing career that he dreaded race day, figuring out that he had to find a “relaxed joy” when competing. He recalled a log sheet from his high school days, when perhaps there was a bit more of a sunnier disposition, reminding him of how things were and Ryan Tripp (left) and Dartmouth head coach Trevor Michelson.

articles.text: Piedmont’s flag football team returns for its third year. Piedmont High’s flag football team returns for their third year of action, getting their season started this Thursday, August 28 against St. Mary’s of Berkeley at Witter Field. The sport has quickly become arguably the most popular sport at the school with more than 50 athletes on varsity and two separate junior varsity squads. “We had over 50 girls tryout and we have enough girls to field a varsity and two junior varsity teams. One of the JV teams is an all-freshman team and will compete in the same league because there are no other freshman teams,” coach Beth Black said. “As we expected, girls who picked up the football found out how quickly they liked the game. We’re running a supportive environment and want to teach kids how to play,” she added. The Highlanders went 6-10 last season and will have to replace All-League players Miya Fujimoto and Dorothy Nemeth. articles.text: For some children, the toughest part of going back to school isn’t meeting a new teacher, finding their classroom, or making friends — it’s speaking up. Answering a question, asking for help, or joining in at lunch can feel overwhelming when communication anxiety takes over. As a pediatric speech-language pathologist, I often meet students who are lively talkers at home but become quiet, hesitant, or even silent in the classroom. The causes vary shyness, past experiences, perfectionism, or a speech and language difference. The good news? With patience, understanding, and a few simple strategies, parents and teachers can help children build confidence. 1. Shyness or Anxiety? Shyness is a personality trait that often eases once a child warms up. Communication anxiety is different: it lingers and can cause kids to avoid speaking altogether. Signs include refusing to raise a hand, freezing or whispering when called on, saying “I don’t know” when they do, and showing physical distress such as fidgeting, blushing, or tearing up before speaking. If these behaviors appear often in school, they may point to more than shyness. 2. Practice in Safe Spaces Role-play common school situations at home: asking to use the restroom, ordering lunch, answering a question. Start small, maybe practicing with stuffed animals or siblings, then build up to a few friends or relatives. The key is gradual exposure in low-pressure settings. 3. Exposure, Not Pressure Telling a child to “just speak up” usually backfires. Instead, set up small wins. Ask for a single word, then a short phrase, then a full answer. Over time, these small successes reduce fear and grow confidence. 4. Build Self-Advocacy Even young children can communicate needs without words. A simple cue card: “I need help” or “I need a break”, allows them to express themselves while reducing stress. As confidence builds, swap cards for spoken requests. 5. Partner Early With Teachers If your child struggles, loop in their teacher at the start of the year. Share strategies: call on your child only for questions

articles.text: California College of the Arts invites teens to explore art & design This fall, California College of the Arts (CCA) is opening its doors to local high school students who want to dive into the world of art and design. From hands-on workshops to the prestigious Scholastic Art & Writing Awards, there are many ways for young artists to explore their passions and showcase their talent. All high school students ages 14 to 18 are welcome to join CCA’s fall Atelier programs. These non-credit weekend intensives and multi-week classes run from October 1 through December 15. Each course is designed to be flexible, inspiring, and taught by practicing artists and designers who understand how to connect with high school students. Atelier classes encourage students to experiment with new materials, sharpen their skills, and create pieces they can proudly include in future art and design school applications. Studios include 2D Portfolio Development, Animation, Architecture and Interior Design, Fashion, Figure Drawing, Illustration, and Industrial Design. Registration is now open, and spots are available on a first-come, first-served basis. For students eager to share their creativity, the Scholastic Art & Writing Awards offer a chance to shine. This national competition is open for submissions from October 1, 2025, through January 6, 2026. Middle and high school students in grades 7 through 12 can enter work in 28 art and writing categories, and high school seniors may also submit complete art portfolios. CCA is proud to host the Bay Area regional chapter for the fourth year in a row and has been inspired by the vision and passion of students who are shaping the future of the creative world. The regional competition concludes with a spring pop-up exhibition at CCA, where award-winning students present their work to friends, family, and the community. Submissions can be entered at artandwriting.org. Students preparing for college Instructor supporting an Atelier student as they build a concept board for their upcoming fashion design project. have another important opportunity this fall. On November 9, 2025, CCA will host National Portfolio Day, featuring more than 30 leading art and design colleges accredited by the National Association of Schools of Art and Design. Representatives will provide in-person and virtual portfolio reviews, answer questions about their programs and admissions, and offer guidance on building a portfolio that stands out. This season is full of possibilities for young artists to learn, create, and take exciting steps toward their future. Join CCA’s vibrant community and watch your teen’s confidence and creativity grow. articles.text: Claude, the iconic American alligator with albinism at the California Academy of Sciences, will be celebrating his 30th birthday (or hatch day) this September. The museum is marking the occasion with a month of daily festivities including merch giveaways, Mascot Claude photo-ops, special programs, and a splashy cupcake party on September 14 to celebrate the reptile who’s captured the hearts and minds of millions. Thirty may sound old, but in human care alligators can live well into their sixties. Claude currently weighs 278 pounds and is over 10 feet long. But back when he first hatched from his egg, Claude was only about the size of a banana. Claude’s pale color is due to albinism, a rare genetic mutation that prevents the production of a pigment called melanin. American alligators are typically black or dark green, but because of his albinism, Claude’s skin is translucent and appears white. Albinism affects his eyes as well, giving him low vision. Claude’s eyes look pinkish red, as the blood vessels in the back of his eyes are visible through his clear irises. Because of his albinism, Claude would not have been able to camouflage well in a natural swamp habitat and would be vulnerable to predators. Many Academy visitors see Claude lying perfectly still in his habitat and wonder if he is real. While he may often look like a Claude will be celebrating his 30th birthday (or hatch day) on September 14 at the California Academy of Sciences. statue, this behavior is typical and advantageous for an alligator. Alligators are ambush predators, relying on camouflage and stealth to save energy by lying in wait until prey comes close enough to lunge. Claude is also a reptile, which means he is ectothermic, or cold blooded, and uses minimal energy to maintain his body temperature. He uses so little energy that he only needs to be fed once a week, and likes to eat fish heads and tails, chicks, rats, and micronutrient gel. In their natural habitat, alligators can go months without eating. American alligators are only found in the Southeastern United States, and are an example of a conservation success story. In the 1960s, commercial hunting and habitat loss drove American alligator populations into decline, and they became an endangered species. But communities near swamps advocated for habitat preserves and hunting regulations, and scientists began alligator breeding programs and investigated alligator biology as well as their role in swamp ecosystems. The museum is marking the occasion with a month of daily festivities including merch giveaways, Mascot Claude photo-ops, special programs, and a splashy cupcake party on September 14 to celebrate the reptile who’s captured the hearts and minds of millions. Thirty may sound old, but in human care alligators can live well into their sixties. Claude currently weighs 278 pounds and is over 10 feet long. But back when he first hatched from his egg, Claude was only about the size of a banana. Claude’s pale color is due to albinism, a rare genetic mutation that prevents the production of a pigment called melanin. American alligators are typically black or dark green, but because of his albinism, Claude’s skin is translucent and appears white. Albinism affects his eyes as well, giving him low vision. Claude’s eyes look pinkish red, as the blood vessels in the back of his eyes are visible through his clear irises. Because of his albinism, Claude would not have been able to camouflage well in a natural swamp habitat and would be vulnerable to predators. Alligators are ambush predators, relying on camouflage and stealth to save energy by lying in wait until prey comes close enough to lunge. Claude is also a reptile, which means he is ectothermic, or cold blooded, and uses minimal energy to maintain his body temperature. He uses so little energy that he only needs to be fed once a week, and likes to eat fish heads and tails, chicks, rats, and micronutrient gel. In their natural habitat, alligators can go months without eating. American alligators are only found in the Southeastern United States, and are an example of a conservation success story. In the 1960s, commercial hunting and habitat loss drove American alligator populations into decline, and they became an endangered species. But communities near swamps advocated for habitat preserves and hunting regulations, and scientists began alligator breeding programs and investigated alligator biology as well as their role in swamp ecosystems. articles.text: Performances in Mountain View, Walnut Creek & San Francisco Smuin Ballet Company presents its fall season, entitled “Extremely Close,” on September 12 with three performances at Mountain View Center for Performing Arts, followed by events in Walnut Creek and San Francisco. Smuin’s 32nd season is directed by Amy Seiwert and is inspired by Alejandro Cerrundo’s art installation and movement drama Extremely Close, set to a score by Philip Glass and Dustin O’Halloran. Fall performances include the West Coast premiere of choreographer Justin Peck’s Partita, set to Caroline Shaw’s Pulitzer Prize-winning “Partita for 8 Voices,” a unique number featuring eight dancers in sneakers. Smuin Ballet will be the first company outside of New York City Ballet to perform the work since it premiered in 2022. The final piece being performed in this season’s fall programming is A Long Night choreographed by Seiwert, a former mentee of the late Michael Smuin. Seiwert reimagines Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream with humor and heartfelt storytelling that honors George Balanchine’s original choreography. A Long Night premiered in 2023 for BalletX in Philadelphia and is set to songs by Patsy Cline, Pink Martini, Harry Nilsson, and more. “To have Justin’s [Peck] and Alejandro’s [Cerrundo] work in my first curated season is an honor and a thrill,” said Seiwert. “Justin’s creative path reminds me a bit of our founder Michael Smuin’s. His work in film and on Broadway informs the distinctive style he brings to his creations for the concert dance stage. And Alejandro’s work exemplifies how extraordinary contemporary dance can be: musical and theatrical, with a mystery that will take your breath away.” Smuin Ballet Company’s fall season opens at the Mountain View Center for the Performing Arts September 12 with performances through September 14: Friday and Saturday at 7:30 p.m., with two additional matinees Saturday and Sunday at 2 p.m. Lesher Center for the Arts in Walnut Creek hosts two performances September 19 through 20: Friday at 7:30 p.m. and Saturday at 2 p.m. The company’s fall season concludes at the Yerba Buena Center for the Arts in San Francisco September 26 through October 5 with eight performances scheduled: Friday, September 26 at 7:30 p.m.; Saturday and Sunday, September 27 and 28 at 2 p.m.; Thursday, October 2 at 7:30 p.m.; Friday, October 3 at 7:30 p.m.; Saturday, October 4 at 2 p.m. and 7:30 p.m.; and Sunday, October 5 at 2 p.m. Single-day tickets are available at www.smuinballet.org. Blake Garden is a little known treasure located at 70 Kenyon Rd. in Kensington, just a 25-minute drive from Piedmont. The Garden is 100 years old and exists because Anson Styles Blake and Anita Day Blake agreed to sell their Berkeley home and property to UC Berkeley so the California Memorial Stadium could be built. Upon completion of the house they were joined by Anita’s sister, Mabel Symmes. Mabel, like her sister and brother-in-law, was a graduate of UC Berkeley where she was a student of Landscape Architecture. Together the sisters set out to design and plant beautiful gardens containing water features, pocket gardens with statuary, Oak trees, a small canyon with Redwood trees, controlled creeks and much, much more. articles.text: Festival Opera continues its 2025 season on August 24 and September 28.with an innovative Salon Series of Sunday afternoon concerts at Piedmont Center for the Arts featuring some of the Bay Area’s rising stars and critically acclaimed artists. The series offers intimate, artist-curated performances that highlight rare repertoire and virtuosic collaboration between talented singers and musicians alike. At the conclusion of each concert, the audience is invited to stay for a post-performance reception with the artists. Festival Opera General Director Zachary Gordin commented, “This new format encourages programming a broader variety of vocal music: art song, arias and scenes from operas, solo cantatas, complete short operas, and even some gems from genres outside of the classical music spectrum. The artists and programs we present this year are all very dear to me, and the singers are absolute stars of their respective voice types. They are sure to offer memorable and impactful performances which our audience can witness up-close in this chamber music venue.” American Song Cycles Last Sunday, August 24, the newly inaugurated Festival Opera Salon Series continued with an afternoon of music by renowned soprano Carrie Hennessey and acclaimed pianist Daniel Lockert featuring two magnificent works by American composers. Concert goers had the chance to experience encore performances of Julia Seeholzer’s Portraits of Disquiet, a reflection on our modern world first performed in Festival Opera’s online recital series during the pandemic, and Jake Heggie’s At the Statue of Venus, a poignant and humorous journey of anticipation and self-discovery which was a part of the company’s 2021 mainstage production. Bel Canto Forever On Sunday, September 28 at 4 p.m., Festival Opera plans a celebration of soaring vocalism with soprano Shawnette Sulker and contralto Sara Couden, accompanied by Zachary Gordin at the piano. The program includes the 19th century Bel Canto music of Rossini, Bellini, Delibes and Meyerbeer with dazzling duets, arias, soaring melodies and vocal fireworks that define the art of bel canto, beautiful singing. Individual tickets for each Salon concert are priced at $40 and available online at www.festivalopera.org. Carrie Hennessey Shawnette Sulker Sara Couden Residency at the Mac In addition to the Salon Series, Festival Opera announces a new residency at Point Richmond’s historic Hotel Mac, presenting a series of “First Fridays” at the newly renovated Biancoverde Restaurant with its menu of sumptuous Italian fare. Zachary Gordin shared, “The series will feel like fun and casual operatic ‘jam sessions’ for the restaurant and bar patrons, bringing favorite opera artists from the Bay Area and beyond to the Mac, performing hits from opera, Broadway, and more.” Upcoming “First Fridays” are scheduled for 6:30 p.m. on September 5, October 3, November 7, and December 5. Artists and programs will be announced. There is no cover charge, but advance reservations are recommended. The iconic Hotel Mac, which originally opened in 1911, is located at 50 Washington Avenue in Point Richmond. For more details and reservations, visit festivalopera.org/at-the-mac.

articles.text: Director Joshua B. Porter Piedmont natives Karyn and Kevin Yarris, alongside director Joshua B. Porter, are set to begin filming their upcoming indie feature film I’ve Got You next month. I’ve Got You is a story of love, loss, hope, redemption, and the enduring power of family. Produced by Piedmont natives Karyn and Kevin Yarris under their Wildwood Entertainment banner, the film promises to deliver an emotionally rich and visually stunning cinematic experience. The romantic drama, written by Kevin Yarris, is now in pre-production and is set to begin filming in Calaveras County in September. “We are thrilled to have Josh at the helm of this project,” said Karyn Yarris. “His vision and passion align perfectly with the heart of this story, and we can’t wait to bring it to life.” Featured in the starring roles are Aaron Dominguez, who acted in Hulu’s Only Murders in the Building and current star of the horror film Witchboard, and Nicholas Cirillo, who boasts credits in Black Mirror, Outer Banks, and She-Hulk: Attorney at Law. The film follows brothers Tyler (Dominguez) and Kyle (Cirillo) on a journey to discover their purpose in life. Along the way, they find themselves and, unexpectedly, love. Karyn Yarris previously served as an executive producer on the feature film Blowback, starring Randy Couture and Cam Gigandet, while Kevin Yarris contributed as a writer on the film. In addition to his work on I’ve Got You, Josh’s debut feature film No Evidence of Man has garnered acclaim winning best screenplay at the Madrid Film Festival and Best Cinematography at the 2025 Golden State Film Festival. For more information, visit ivegotyouthemovie.com. Co-star Aaron Dominguez Producer Karyn Yarris Co-star Nicholas Cirillo Writer/Producer Kevin Yarris

articles.text: Registration is open for the Fall 2025 session of Piedmont Adult School. The session will start September 8 and run through December 20. The fall session will include a wide range of classes in Art, Business, Computers/Tech, Cooking, Exercise, Language, Music, Philosophy and more. Among the new classes offered this fall is “Philosophy for Life,” taught by Stephen Szczepanek. The course will cover the teachings of philosophers ranging from Plato to Descartes to Kant, giving students a solid grounding in philosophical thought and a basis to explore independently. “Philosophy is a way for us to engage deeply with the most difficult questions of human existence: who we are, what our purpose is on this planet, and what it means to live a fulfilled, authentic life,” said Szczepanek. A native of England, Szczepanek holds Bachelor’s and Master’s degrees in Philosophy from the University of Oxford. He will also be teaching Conversational Intermediate Spanish for the Adult School. In addition to Spanish, he speaks French, Italian, Greek and Polish. Stephen Szczepanek will teach a course at Piedmont Adult School titled Philosophy for Life, an overview of world philosophers. “Teaching new ways to communicate and understand the world is a real joy for me,” said Szczepanek. “That’s why I love to share the gift of philosophy and languages.” Come learn something new, expand your horizons, and meet great people in a friendly, lowstress environment. Check out all the classes and register online at Piedmontadultschool.org, or by calling 594-2655. Classes do fill up, so register right away for best availability. pages.text: 28 Wednesday, August 27, 2025 Walking on Wednesday Piedmont Walkers tour city landmarks with new Police Chief By Dick Carter There was a strong turnout of 45 walkers and three K-9 best friends at the Exedra last Wednesday for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s weekly Walking on Wednesdays outing. The group also welcomed two special first-time walkers: new Piedmont Police Chief Frederick W. Shavies II and his assistant, April Fitzgerald. Before the walk began, Chief Shavies was introduced. He grew up in Oakland and attended Fremont High School, where he was an All-City football player. He went on to Washington State University, playing defensive end and appearing in the Rose Bowl. After graduation, he joined the Oakland Police Department in 2006, rising to Deputy Chief. He Walking on Wednesday group in motion was appointed Piedmont’s police chief in July. Shavies has children in Piedmont schools and has already embraced the community. He registered with the Recreation Department for Walking on Wednesdays and plans to walk with the group when his schedule allows. The walkers started behind the Exedra, past Community Hall and the Tea House, and up the Highland-Guilford steps in Piedmont Park. The $155,000 project, completed in 2023 with support from the Piedmont Beautification Foundation, replaced wooden railroad ties with concrete steps, landings and handrails. The steps now provide a handsome entrance to the park. The group emerged on Highland Avenue, where Chief Shavies helped them cross, and continued up Sierra Avenue. On Sierra, a Julia Morgan-designed home was undergoing major foundation work. From there the group walked Sheridan Avenue, Wildwood Avenue, the Hall Fenway, Crocker Avenue and Hampton Road, stopping for a photo with the chief at King Avenue. They continued on to Hampton Park and up Hampton to Lexford and Huntleigh Roads. At LaSalle Avenue, they entered the St. James Woods Terrace neighborhood, marked by its early 20th-century white pillars and distinctive terracotta tile sidewalk inlays. At Lexford and Hampton, the group saw one of two designated Piedmont Heritage Tree Southern magnolias, with the second located nearby on Huntleigh. The Heritage Tree Program, established in 2018 by the City Council on the Park Commission’s recommendation, has recognized 28 trees citywide. The walk also featured a 1939 Storybook-style brick home on Lexford Road, designed by architect and engineer Carr Jones. The house features a circular chimney, a wavy brick wall, a terracotta and slate roof, and a turret that gives it a castle-like appearChief Shavies walks with Dick Carter ance. A sign at the door reads, “The rooster crows, but the hen delivers.” Architect and walker Jim Kellogg shared details about the house, including its unique brick garage addition and pool in the back. The owner, Eric Tupper, came out to greet the group, explaining that it was his wife’s childhood home. Their children built the brick maze in the yard during the pandemic. He added that the home’s radiant heating is its best feature. The group enjoyed meeting Tupper and learning about the home before heading back through Hampton, LaSalle and St. James Drive, and returning to the town center. It was a longer walk than usual, but especially memorable with Chief Shavies and Fitzgerald joining in and providing a police escort throughout. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at 10:30 a.m. at the Exedra (Highland and Magnolia Avenues). Everyone is welcome to join, and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially encouraged. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu or by calling (510) 420-3070. New Piedmont Police Chief Frederick W. articles.text: Carleton Denis “Denny” Mathewson passed away peacefully at home on August 6, 2025, at the age of 88. Denny was born in San Francisco on November 21, 1936 – Big Game day – a fitting beginning for someone who loved college football and whose life would be marked by spirited optimism, light hearted humor, and unwavering love for his family and friends. Denny began his education at St. Dominic’s Elementary School, with a formative three-year stay in Eureka while his father served in World War II. He later attended St. Ignatius High School in San Francisco and graduated from Stanford University in 1958 with a degree in Economics. After college, he served in the U.S. Army before starting his professional life at The Emporium, which sent him to New York on a special assignment. After a year in New York, he returned to California and established a long and respected career in commercial real estate. In retirement, he served on the Piedmont Education Foundation Board and volunteered for Experience Corps as a tutor, working with kids in Oakland schools. Denny approached life with a positive outlook, a sense of humor, and a curiosity in others. He had a natural ease and all felt welcome in his presence. A gifted storyteller, he had a knack for bringing people together through laughter, memory, and warmth. He had a deep appreciation for life’s simple pleasures and was happiest spending time on the ski slopes or at the beach with his friends and family. He Denny Mathewson passed away at the age of 88. and his wife, Jan, shared a love of travel and saw much of the world together. More than anything, Denny adored his family. He was a proud and devoted husband, father, and grandfather, and found true joy in the lives and accomplishments of his children and grandchildren. He is survived by his wife Jan; daughters Hilary Anne Conrad and Lindsey Ziegler; son-inlaw Brad Ziegler; and beloved grandchildren Clemens and Bay Conrad, and Clara and Cameron Ziegler. He was preceded in death by parents, Dr. Carleton Mathewson, Jr. and Catherine Daly Mathewson and sisters Anne Mathewson Wood and Shelagh Mae Denning. A celebration of life will be held in October. In lieu of flowers, the family encourages donations to The Cancer League, Inc. or the Piedmont Education Foundation in Denny’s memory.

I’m thrilled to have reached this milestone.” Recent efforts have focused on completing the site’s landscaping – everything has to be planted before pools can be filled with water, in order to avoid stains while the pool’s white plaster cures underwater. The City has a walkthrough with the Alameda County Department of Environmental Health scheduled for Wednesday, August 27. If all goes well, crews will begin the 3-day process of plastering and filling the pools on Tuesday, September 2nd. Project leadership previously projected the pools to be filled with water in the last week of August, at the August 4 City Council meeting. After construction is complete and the pools are filled with water, the pool still will not be ready to open until the site has gone through system testing, also known as “commissioning.” Commissioning can take as little as six weeks, or much longer if significant issues are identified that need to be resolved.
